opening_message:
Ticket 1: Jacob Santos (employee ID E050) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E050.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Jacob Santos (E050) is a full-time Engineer requesting write access to Source Code. As an Engineer, he owns the Source Code system; requested write access is within policy. Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E050 is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training; never admin. Since training is basic, max access is read. Note: this differs from HR note (full_time), but Security DB is authoritative for employment/training. Recommend read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee E050 (Jacob Santos) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory has two notes with conflicting information:

Note 1 (HR): role Engineer, employment type full_time, recommendation write. As full-time Engineer owns Source Code, write is within policy.

Note 2 (Security): role Engineer, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation read. Contractors: read, or write only with advanced training; never admin. Training is basic, so max is read.

The Security note says Security DB is authoritative for employment/training.

So conflicting employment type: full_time vs contractor. Security DB is authoritative → contractor with basic training → max access is read.

Requested level: write. Maximum: read. Since requested is above maximum, grant the maximum = read.

So submit read.
